messages.author: c454b293eaa50635
messages.subject: inlabru predictions for years not in the original data set
parts:
Hello. Apologies if this is too basic. I am fitting a spatiotemporal model for 18 years (i.e. 2000 to 2018) of health data across 246 regions within 8 countries. I have successfully managed to replicate my inla model using bru(). When I make predictions using a new data set with the same years as in the original set I manage to run the code without problems. However, if I want to compute predictions for a year not in the data set (e.g. 2020) then I get the following error:

Error in Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = seq_len(N), j = idx, x = rep(1, N),  : 
  all(dims >= dims.min) is not TRUE

Is there a way to overcome this issue?

My code looks like this:

n_locs  <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.area1))
n_count <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.country))
n_month <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.month))
n_years <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.year))

f1 <- total ~
  f(ID.area, model='besag', graph=H) +
  site(map=ID.area1, model="iid", n=n_locs) +
  cnts(map=ID.country, model="iid", n=n_count) +
  rseas(map=ID.month, model="iid", n=n_month) +
  rtrend(map=ID.year, model="iid", n=n_years) +
  tas02 + pre02 + hur02 + population_density

mod1 <- bru(as.formula(f1),
            family="nbinomial",
            data=bru_vars,
            options=list(offset(log(bru_vars$population)),
                         control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian", 
                                           int.strategy="eb")))

Any help will be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Felipe

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inlabru predictions for years not in the original data set
parts:
Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

On Tuesday, September 29, 2020 at 12:57:58 PM UTC+1 felipe...@googlemail.com wrote:
Hello. Apologies if this is too basic. I am fitting a spatiotemporal model for 18 years (i.e. 2000 to 2018) of health data across 246 regions within 8 countries. I have successfully managed to replicate my inla model using bru(). When I make predictions using a new data set with the same years as in the original set I manage to run the code without problems. However, if I want to compute predictions for a year not in the data set (e.g. 2020) then I get the following error:

Error in Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = seq_len(N), j = idx, x = rep(1, N),  : 
  all(dims >= dims.min) is not TRUE

Is there a way to overcome this issue?

My code looks like this:

n_locs  <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.area1))
n_count <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.country))
n_month <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.month))

  tas02 + pre02 + hur02 + population_density

mod1 <- bru(as.formula(f1),

            data=bru_vars,
            options=list(offset(log(bru_vars$population)),
                         control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian", 
                                           int.strategy="eb")))

Any help will be greatly appreciated.

Felipe

Hmmm,
I note that 246 isn't equal to either 18 or 100. Can you check what all the n_*-variables you use actually are set to, to help narrow it down?
But first, please install the inlabru devel version, as several odd bugs have been fixed in that version (see https://github.com/fbachl/inlabru/ for instructions)
and rerun your last version of the code again (with _no_ new changes, so that we can know for sure if it's the inlabru version that makes a difference, in case it works).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

On Tuesday, September 29, 2020 at 1:41:33 PM UTC+1 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

On Tuesday, September 29, 2020 at 12:57:58 PM UTC+1 felipe...@googlemail.com wrote:
Hello. Apologies if this is too basic. I am fitting a spatiotemporal model for 18 years (i.e. 2000 to 2018) of health data across 246 regions within 8 countries. I have successfully managed to replicate my inla model using bru(). When I make predictions using a new data set with the same years as in the original set I manage to run the code without problems. However, if I want to compute predictions for a year not in the data set (e.g. 2020) then I get the following error:

Error in Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = seq_len(N), j = idx, x = rep(1, N),  : 
  all(dims >= dims.min) is not TRUE

Is there a way to overcome this issue?

My code looks like this:

n_locs  <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.area1))
n_count <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.country))
n_month <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.month))
n_years <- length(unique(bru_vars$ID.year))

f1 <- total ~
  f(ID.area, model='besag', graph=H) +
  site(map=ID.area1, model="iid", n=n_locs) +
  cnts(map=ID.country, model="iid", n=n_count) +
  rseas(map=ID.month, model="iid", n=n_month) +
  rtrend(map=ID.year, model="iid", n=n_years) +
  tas02 + pre02 + hur02 + population_density

mod1 <- bru(as.formula(f1),
            family="nbinomial",
            data=bru_vars,
            options=list(offset(log(bru_vars$population)),
                         control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian", 
                                           int.strategy="eb")))

Any help will be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Felipe

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn

Hi,

the n-value needs to be the largest index (including those those that are only used for prediction), not the number of unique indices. Change length(unique(...)) to max(...) of all values, both those used for estimation and those used in prediction.  (And the indices need to start at 1)
It can't predict for coordinates not covered in the estimation, so the bru() model needs to include the years you want to predict (as in the components need to contain them, even if the data itself doesn't have observations for them).

Finn
